description: I’m Moez, a software engineer from Pakistan with experience in Python data pipelines and backend development. We’re building a tool that lets users pick a region and an Earth science variable, starting with heat index from NASA MERRA-2 data, plot how it changes over the years, and test if the trend is significant using the Mann-Kendall test. Join us if you enjoy climate data, statistics, Python, or web visualization. We’re looking for data analysts, statisticians, and web developers.
summary: HeatPOD Trend Detective is a free web app that helps students and the public investigate how Earth’s climate is changing, using 45 years (1981 to 2025) of daily NASA POWER data based on NASA MERRA-2. Users pick a variable (air temperature, daily maximum temperature, humidity, rainfall or heat index) and a region, then follow five guided steps, like a detective’s case file. The app removes the seasonal cycle, plots the time series, measures the rate of change, and tests significance with an autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall test, a 95% confidence interval and a false discovery rate correction across the map. To show where trends differ, it uses Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) to split the map into repeating patterns. To check whether the worst days are getting worse, it tests the trend in each year’s hottest day and compares extreme value (GEV) return levels. Two demos show the results: Florida warmed 0.33 °C per decade with every land square rising, while in the dry Phoenix region the hottest day of the year rose 0.31 °C per decade (p = 0.018). Every result is explained in plain words, so anyone can tell a real trend from random noise.
details:
What it does and how it works

HeatPOD Trend Detective is a web app that turns 45 years of NASA data into clear answers about climate change in a specific place. A user picks a variable (air temperature, daily maximum temperature, relative humidity, rainfall or heat index) and a region, then follows five guided steps:

  1. What: choose a variable, with a plain definition of what it measures and why it matters.
  2. Where: choose a region. Two demos are ready: Florida (humid heat) and the Phoenix region, Arizona (dry heat).
  3. Evidence: the app removes the seasonal cycle, plots the monthly differences from normal, and fits a trend line. It reports the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence interval, and tests significance with a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation (months that depend on each other). Sen’s slope gives a robust second estimate.
  4. Patterns: a trend map shows every grid square, using a false discovery rate correction so squares that look significant by chance are greyed out. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) then splits 45 years of maps into a few repeating patterns, showing where parts of a region move together or in opposite directions.
  5. Extremes: the app takes the most extreme day of each year, tests whether it is trending, and fits Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) curves to compare how often a 20-year extreme happens now versus before.

Every result ends in a plain-language verdict, for example: “Air temperature has risen by 0.33 °C per decade since 1981. This trend is very unlikely to be chance (p < 0.001).”

Results from the demos

  • Florida’s air temperature rose 0.33 °C per decade, and all 42 land squares are rising significantly.
  • POD shows that 91% of Florida’s variation is the whole state moving together, while a second pattern (6%) shows north and south Florida moving in opposite directions.
  • In the dry Phoenix region the hottest day of the year rose 0.31 °C per decade (p = 0.018). Florida’s heat index extremes rise in half its squares, but are not yet significant for the region as a whole.

Benefits and intended impact

The tool lets students, teachers and the public do real climate analysis without writing code or downloading data. It teaches them to tell a real trend from random noise, and shows that one region can contain different trends. We hope it is used in classrooms and by local communities to understand heat risk where they live.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA POWER daily API (based on NASA MERRA-2), 1981 to 2025, about 55 km grid
  • Language: Python
  • Data and statistics: xarray, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, regionmask
  • Web app: Streamlit with Altair charts, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud
  • Engineering: GitHub Actions runs automated tests on every change, and only code that passes is released to the live app

How it is creative

The app is designed like a detective’s case file: numbered investigation steps, a verdict stamp (“SIGNIFICANT” or “NOT SIGNIFICANT”), and margin notes that explain each term next to the chart that uses it. It combines methods usually found only in research papers (POD and extreme value theory) with a simple guided flow anyone can follow.

Factors we considered

  • Statistical honesty: we correct for autocorrelation and for testing many squares at once, and we show “not significant” results as clearly as significant ones.
  • Accessibility: colorblind-safe colors (blue to red, never rainbow), grey for non-significant areas, and plain definitions for a high school audience.
  • Reliability: all analysis is precomputed, so the app never depends on a live data download during use.
  • Limitations: the grid is about 55 km, the data comes from a model rather than weather stations, and the heat index combines daily maximum temperature with daily average humidity, so it is an approximation.

Links

  • Live app: https://heatpod-trend-detective.streamlit.app/
  • Code: https://github.com/moezalikhan/heatpod-trend-detective
